pages.name: Drift or noise
pages.task: One cell's quarterly readings rise six times in a row. Is that drift or noise?
pages.answer: Drift, because a run of six one way is rare by chance
pages.why: Noise goes up and down at random. Each new reading is about as likely to fall as to rise. So six rises in a row seldom happens by chance. A run of six one way is the usual signal that something is pushing the readings.

pages.name: Its own baseline
pages.text: Judge each cell against its own first reading, not against its neighbours. Here is a string of 24 cells. Each cell is read for impedance every quarter. Its first reading, at commissioning, is its [[baseline]]. Cells differ from new, here from 0.46 to 0.54 mΩ. So one reading on its own says little about a cell's health. Most resistance-based testers predict health little better than tossing a coin. Here cell 17 sits flat on its 0.50 mΩ baseline at quarter 8.

pages.name: Which cell to watch
pages.task: Cell A was commissioned at 0.46 mΩ and now reads 0.53 mΩ. Cell B started at 0.54 mΩ and still reads 0.54 mΩ. The string averages 0.50 mΩ. Which cell should you watch?
pages.answer: A, because it has risen about 15% from its own baseline
pages.why: Judge each cell against its own first reading. A started at 0.46 mΩ and now reads 0.53 mΩ. That is 0.07 mΩ up, about 15%. B has read 0.54 mΩ since it was new. That is just how it was made. So A is the cell to watch.

pages.name: The turn upward
pages.text: A steady climb one way is [[drift]], not noise. As the quarters run on, cell 17 stays flat for ten quarters. It wobbles a little like the rest. Then it turns upward by 0.02 mΩ a quarter and keeps going. The fitted slope through its last four readings rises from about zero to 0.020 mΩ a quarter. By quarter 15 cell 17 reads 0.60 mΩ. That is 20% above its own baseline, and 5 SDs from the string's mean.

pages.name: How far it has risen
pages.task: A cell's baseline was 0.50 mΩ, and it now reads 0.60 mΩ. How far has it risen from its baseline?
pages.why: The rise is the reading take away the baseline, so 0.60 − 0.50 = 0.10 mΩ. Divide that by the baseline. 0.10 ÷ 0.50 = 0.2, and 0.2 is 20%.

pages.name: The test decides
pages.text: A [[capacity test]] decides. The example string is rated 200 Ah at the 10-hour rate, so it is discharged at 20 A. The clock runs until the string reaches its end voltage. At a fixed current, ampere-hours are amps × hours. So capacity is the hours run ÷ 10 hours. The replacement line is 80%, at 8 hours. The weakest cell sets how long the string lasts. At quarter 15 the clock stops at 7.8 hours. That is 78%, short of the line.

pages.name: Reading the test
pages.task: A string rated for 10 hours at 20 A reaches its end voltage after 8.5 hours. What does the test say?
pages.answer: 85% of rated capacity, above the 80% line, so keep it and keep trending
pages.why: At a fixed current, ampere-hours are amps × hours. So the share of its rating is 8.5 ÷ 10 = 85%. Every battery loses some capacity with age. The replacement line is 80%, so this string stays. Keep trending it, and the trend says when to test next.

pages.name: What the charging did
pages.text: The trend says which cell. The test says how much it has lost. The charging record says why. Keep a cell short of full charge, and soft sulphate hardens into crystals on the negative plate. Leave it at low charge with shallow cycles, and the acid sinks and starves the tops of the plates. Float it too high for too long, and the positive grid softens and sheds. Charge a valve-regulated cell too hard, and it vents its gas and dries out. Here the cell shows [[sulphation]].

pages.task: A flooded string's float was set below the maker's band for a year. Which fault should you expect?
pages.why: On float a cell should stay fully charged. Below the band it never quite gets there. So the soft lead sulphate is never fully turned back. Over months it hardens into crystals on the negative plates.

pages.name: What can still be done
pages.text: Each fault leaves a different job. An [[equalising charge]] is a deliberate overcharge of the whole string. It reverses sulphation that is caught in time. Its gassing also mixes stratified acid. Grid corrosion is permanent. A valve-regulated cell cannot be topped up, so dry-out stays. So the earlier the trend finds a cell, the more can still be saved. Here each fault carries its tag.

pages.name: All together
pages.task: Every cell in a flooded string has risen about 25% from its own baseline, all together. Cell 9 sits 0.3 SD from the string's mean. Is the string healthy?
pages.answer: No, the whole string has drifted, so test its capacity
pages.why: The z-score compares a cell with its neighbours. When every cell climbs together, the mean climbs with them. So no cell looks odd. Each cell's own baseline still shows a 25% rise. That is past the 20% line, so test the string's capacity.

pages.name: Boosted for weeks
pages.task: A valve-regulated string was left on boost charge for weeks. Now one cell's impedance climbs. Which fault fits, and will an equalise help?
pages.answer: Dry-out, and an equalise would make it worse
pages.why: Weeks of boost charge are far too much charge. The cell gassed, and its valve let the gas out. A valve-regulated cell cannot be topped up, so that water is gone. An equalise is more overcharge, so it would dry the cell further.
